questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a rate limiter in a distributed system?
options: To encrypt API traffic between clients and servers
To control the number of requests a client can make in a given time period
To compress request payloads for faster transmission
To route requests to the least-loaded server
questions.explanation: A rate limiter controls request frequency per client or per endpoint within a time window. This prevents abuse, protects backend resources from being overwhelmed, ensures fair usage across clients, and helps control infrastructure costs.

questions.question: In the token bucket algorithm, what happens when a request arrives and the bucket is empty?
options: The request is queued until a token becomes available
The request is rejected or throttled immediately
A new bucket is created for the overflow
The token refill rate is temporarily increased
questions.explanation: When the token bucket is empty, there are no tokens to consume, so the request is rejected (typically with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests). The bucket continues refilling at its configured rate, and future requests will be allowed once tokens are available.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of the token bucket algorithm over fixed window counting?
options: Token bucket uses less memory
Token bucket allows controlled bursts while maintaining an average rate
Token bucket is easier to implement in distributed systems
Token bucket provides exact per-second precision
questions.explanation: Token bucket naturally handles bursts — if the bucket has accumulated tokens, a client can use them in a quick burst, then settle back to the steady refill rate. Fixed window counting has no burst concept and suffers from the boundary problem where limits can be doubled.

questions.question: What is the 'boundary problem' with fixed window rate limiting?
options: Requests at network boundaries are counted twice
A client can send double the allowed requests by timing them at the edge of two consecutive windows
The window size cannot be smaller than one second
Fixed windows cannot track requests from multiple IP addresses
questions.explanation: If a client sends the maximum allowed requests at the end of one window and the maximum at the start of the next, they effectively double the rate limit within a short time span around the boundary. Sliding window algorithms solve this by weighting counts across windows.

questions.question: Why is Redis commonly chosen as the backing store for distributed rate limiters?
options: Redis supports SQL queries for complex rate limiting rules
Redis provides atomic operations like INCR and fast in-memory access with key expiration
Redis automatically distributes rate limits across multiple data centers
Redis is the only database that supports time-based keys
questions.explanation: Redis provides atomic increment (INCR), automatic key expiration (EXPIRE), and sub-millisecond latency since it operates in-memory. These features make it ideal for counters that need to be shared across multiple application servers with minimal overhead.

questions.question: How do Redis Lua scripts help prevent race conditions in distributed rate limiting?
options: Lua scripts encrypt the counter values to prevent tampering
Lua scripts execute read-check-increment atomically on the Redis server in a single operation
Lua scripts replicate counter values across all Redis nodes simultaneously
Lua scripts create separate counters for each application server
questions.explanation: A Redis Lua script runs atomically on the server side — it reads the counter, checks against the limit, and increments if allowed, all in one indivisible operation. This eliminates the race condition where two servers read the same counter value and both allow a request.

questions.question: What is the trade-off between placing a rate limiter at the API gateway versus inside the application?
options: Gateway limiters are faster; application limiters are slower
Gateway limiters provide broad protection early; application limiters enable fine-grained per-user or per-endpoint control
Gateway limiters work only for HTTP; application limiters work for all protocols
Gateway limiters are stateless; application limiters are stateful
questions.explanation: An API gateway rate limiter catches abusive traffic before it reaches any service, providing efficient broad protection. Application-level limiters can apply different rules per user tier, per endpoint, or per resource, but the traffic has already entered the system. Many architectures use both.

questions.question: A token bucket has capacity 100 and refill rate 10 tokens/second. The bucket is full. A burst of 150 requests arrives in 1 second. How many are allowed?
options: 100 requests
110 requests
150 requests
10 requests
questions.explanation: The bucket starts with 100 tokens and gains 10 more during the 1-second burst window, for a total of 110 tokens available. So 110 requests are allowed and 40 are rejected. The bucket is then empty and will refill at 10 tokens/second.

questions.question: In a multi-region deployment, each region has its own Redis for rate limiting. A client with a global limit of 100 req/min sends requests to both regions. What problem arises?
options: Redis instances in different regions will have different clock times
Each region tracks its own counter independently, so the client effectively gets double the global limit
Network latency between regions makes rate limiting impossible
Redis does not support multi-region deployments
questions.explanation: With independent Redis instances per region, a client can send 100 requests to Region A and 100 to Region B, effectively bypassing the 100 req/min global limit. Solutions include cross-region counter synchronization, a centralized rate limiter, or splitting the limit across regions.

questions.question: Your rate limiter should 'fail open' in most cases. When would 'fail closed' (deny all traffic) be the better choice?
options: When the system is under normal operating conditions
When protecting critical financial transactions or security-sensitive endpoints where over-admission is dangerous
When the rate limiter is deployed at the API gateway
When using the token bucket algorithm instead of sliding window
questions.explanation: For security-sensitive systems like payment processing or authentication endpoints, allowing unlimited traffic during a rate limiter failure could enable fraud or brute-force attacks. Fail closed protects against these threats, even though it temporarily blocks legitimate users.
